title: What Is a Standard Drink? Sizes, ABV Math, and Limits by Country
excerpt: A US standard drink is 14 grams of pure alcohol. See what that means for beer, wine, liquor, and cocktails, how to count any drink, and how other countries differ.
metaDescription: A US standard drink is 14 g of alcohol: 12 oz beer, 5 oz wine, or 1.5 oz liquor. How to count any drink, a full chart, and how other countries compare.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The answer first:** in the United States, one standard drink is any drink that contains **14 grams of pure alcohol**, which is about 0.6 fluid ounces. That's roughly the alcohol in a 12-ounce regular beer (about 5% alcohol), a 5-ounce glass of wine (about 12%), or a 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor (40%). The definition is about the alcohol, not the glass. A tall craft IPA, a generous home pour of wine, or a cocktail with two shots in it can each count as two standard drinks or more, even though they look like "one drink."

**Why it matters:** every piece of drinking guidance you'll read, from "one drink an hour" to daily and weekly limits to blood alcohol estimates, is written in standard drinks. If you count by glasses instead, you can be off by half or more without realizing it. This guide shows you the definition in each major country, a ten-second way to work out the number for any drink, a reference chart for common drinks, and what the counts mean for your night and your next morning.

> **A quick safety note.** Standard drinks are a counting tool, not a safety guarantee. The same number of drinks affects people very differently depending on body size, sex, food, medications, and how fast you drink. Don't drive after drinking, even if you think you're under a limit. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if someone who has been drinking** is confused or can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and it's always better to call and be wrong than to wait.

## What Is a Standard Drink? The Official US Definition

A standard drink is a fixed amount of pure alcohol (ethanol) that health agencies use as a common unit, so that beer, wine, spirits, and everything in between can be compared on the same scale.

In the US, the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), the CDC, and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans all use the same figure: **14 grams of pure alcohol**, or about **0.6 fluid ounces**. Each of these contains roughly that amount:

- **12 oz of regular beer** at about 5% alcohol
- **8 to 9 oz of malt liquor** at about 7% alcohol
- **5 oz of table wine** at about 12% alcohol
- **3 to 4 oz of fortified wine** (port, sherry) at about 17 to 20%
- **1.5 oz of 80-proof spirits** (vodka, gin, whiskey, rum, tequila) at 40% alcohol

The pattern is simple: the stronger the drink, the smaller the pour that equals one standard drink. Notice that the familiar "one beer, one glass of wine, one shot" rule only works when the beer is about 5%, the wine is about 12%, and the pours are exactly those sizes. In real life, they often aren't.

### Where 14 grams comes from

You can check the number yourself. Twelve ounces of 5% beer contains 12 × 0.05 = 0.6 ounces of pure alcohol. That's about 17.7 milliliters, and since alcohol weighs about 0.789 grams per milliliter, it comes out to roughly 14 grams. The same math gives you 0.6 ounces from 5 ounces of 12% wine and from 1.5 ounces of 40% liquor. That's why those three drinks are treated as equal.

## How to Calculate Standard Drinks in Any Drink

You only need two numbers: the **volume** of the drink and its **ABV** (alcohol by volume, the percentage printed on the label). Proof in the US is simply double the ABV, so 80 proof means 40%.

**The ounces method (US):**

> Standard drinks = ounces × ABV (as a decimal) ÷ 0.6

Example: a 16-ounce can of 7% IPA is 16 × 0.07 = 1.12 ounces of alcohol. Divide by 0.6 and you get about **1.9 standard drinks**.

**The milliliters method (works anywhere):**

> Grams of alcohol = milliliters × ABV (as a decimal) × 0.789

Then divide by your country's standard drink size: 14 for the US, 10 for Australia, 8 for a UK unit. Example: a 175 mL glass of 13% wine contains 175 × 0.13 × 0.789 ≈ 18 grams of alcohol. That's about **1.3 US standard drinks**, **1.8 Australian standard drinks**, or **2.3 UK units**.

**The UK shortcut:** units = milliliters × ABV (as a percentage) ÷ 1,000. A 568 mL pint of 5% lager is 568 × 5 ÷ 1,000 ≈ **2.8 units**.

If you'd rather skip the arithmetic, our [alcohol content by drink guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-content-by-drink) lists typical ABVs for beer styles, wines, and spirits, so you can plug in realistic numbers.

## Standard Drink Chart: Common Drinks, Counted Honestly

Here's how familiar drinks work out in US standard drinks (14 g). Numbers are rounded and assume typical strengths. Always check the actual ABV on what you're drinking.

| Drink | Typical size | Typical ABV | US standard drinks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light beer | 12 oz | 4.2% | about 0.8 |
| Regular beer or lager | 12 oz | 5% | 1.0 |
| Pint of regular beer | 16 oz | 5% | about 1.3 |
| IPA | 16 oz | 7% | about 1.9 |
| Double IPA or strong ale | 16 oz | 9% | about 2.4 |
| Hard seltzer | 12 oz | 5% | 1.0 |
| Hard cider | 12 oz | 5% | 1.0 |
| Malt liquor | 40 oz | 8% | about 5.3 |
| Glass of wine (standard pour) | 5 oz | 12% | 1.0 |
| Restaurant pour of red | 6 oz | 13.5% | about 1.4 |
| Generous home pour | 9 oz | 13.5% | about 2.0 |
| Bottle of wine | 750 mL | 13.5% | about 5.7 |
| Port or sherry | 3 oz | 20% | 1.0 |
| Sake | 6 oz | 15% | 1.5 |
| Shot of liquor | 1.5 oz | 40% | 1.0 |
| Shot of overproof rum | 1.5 oz | 75% | about 1.9 |
| Fifth of liquor | 750 mL | 40% | about 17 |
| Handle of liquor | 1.75 L | 40% | about 39 |

A few rows tend to surprise people. A bottle of wine shared between two people is close to three standard drinks each, not two. A "pint" of craft beer at a brewery can easily be two drinks. And a fifth of vodka holds about seventeen standard drinks, which is why sharing one among a small group adds up much faster than it feels. For the full wine breakdown, see [how many drinks are in a bottle of wine](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-in-a-bottle-of-wine), and for pour sizes in bars, see [how much alcohol is in a shot](/never-hungover/how-much-alcohol-is-in-a-shot).

## Standard Drink Size of Beer

Beer is where "one drink" drifts the most, because both the size and the strength vary widely.

- **Light beers** are usually around 4 to 4.2% ABV, so a 12-ounce can is a little under one standard drink.
- **Regular lagers and most mainstream beers** sit around 4.5 to 5%, so a 12-ounce can or bottle is about one.
- **Craft beers** often run 6 to 8%, and imperial stouts, barleywines, and double IPAs can reach 9 to 12% or higher. A 16-ounce can of a 9% hazy double IPA is close to two and a half standard drinks.
- **Pints** in a US bar are typically 16 ounces, which is a third more than a 12-ounce standard. A British imperial pint is 568 mL (about 19.2 US ounces), so a pint of 5% beer in a London pub is about 1.6 US standard drinks or 2.8 UK units.

**Non-alcoholic beer** labeled under 0.5% ABV is a tiny fraction of a standard drink. You'd need more than ten 12-ounce cans of 0.5% beer to reach the alcohol in one regular beer. Our guide to [whether non-alcoholic beer has alcohol](/never-hungover/does-non-alcoholic-beer-have-alcohol) covers the details for people who need to avoid alcohol completely.

## Standard Drink Size of Wine

The US standard pour for wine is 5 ounces at 12%. Two things push the real number higher.

First, **wine has gotten stronger.** Many reds today are 13.5 to 15% ABV, and some are higher. A 5-ounce pour of 14.5% Zinfandel is about 1.2 standard drinks, not one.

Second, **pours have gotten bigger.** Restaurants often pour 6 ounces, and at home it's easy to fill a large modern glass with 8 or 9 ounces without noticing. Researchers at the University of Cambridge have documented that the average English wine glass has grown dramatically over the past few centuries, and large glasses make generous pours feel normal.

If you want to keep count, try this once: measure 5 ounces of water into your usual wine glass and look at how far it reaches. Most people are surprised by how little it looks.

## Standard Drink Size of Liquor

A US standard shot is **1.5 ounces of 80-proof (40%) spirits**, which is exactly one standard drink. The tricky parts:

- **Not all spirits are 40%.** Many bourbons and gins are bottled at 45 to 50%, cask-strength whiskey can exceed 60%, and overproof rums reach 75%. A 1.5-ounce pour of 50% whiskey is 1.25 standard drinks.
- **Not all pours are 1.5 ounces.** Shot glasses range from about 1 to 2 ounces, and many bars pour 1.25 to 2 ounces as their standard. A "double" is usually 3 ounces, or two standard drinks at minimum.
- **Free pouring at home** is the biggest source of error. Pouring whiskey "neat" or mixing a drink without a jigger often lands at 2 to 3 ounces.

Flavored liqueurs go the other way: many sit around 15 to 30% ABV, so a 1.5-ounce pour can be well under one standard drink. Check the label.

## How Many Standard Drinks Are in a Cocktail?

Cocktails are the hardest drinks to count, because most contain more than one alcoholic ingredient and many contain more than one shot. Rough estimates for typical recipes:

- **Gin and tonic or vodka soda** with a 1.5-ounce pour: about 1. With a heavy pour: 1.5 or more.
- **Margarita** (tequila plus orange liqueur): commonly about 1.5 to 2, and large restaurant margaritas can be more.
- **Martini** (about 2.5 ounces of gin or vodka plus a splash of vermouth): close to 2.
- **Manhattan or Old Fashioned** (2 ounces of whiskey plus a little vermouth or sugar): about 1.5.
- **Long Island Iced Tea** (several half-ounce spirit pours): commonly around 2 or more.
- **Mojito, daiquiri, or rum and coke** with a standard pour: about 1 to 1.5.

The rule of thumb: count the spirit pours, add up the ounces of 40% liquor, and divide by 1.5. A cocktail with "two shots" is two standard drinks before you count any liqueur. Sweet, cold, or fizzy mixers also make alcohol harder to taste, which is part of why cocktails sneak up on people. The NIAAA's Rethinking Drinking website has a free cocktail content calculator if you want to check a specific recipe.

## Standard Drinks in Ready-to-Drink Cans: Hard Seltzer, Canned Cocktails, and Spiked Drinks

Canned drinks have made counting both easier and harder. Easier, because the volume and ABV are printed on the can. Harder, because the range is huge.

- Most **hard seltzers** are 12 ounces at about 4.5 to 5%, so roughly one standard drink each. Some "extra" versions run 8% or more, which makes them about 1.6.
- **Canned cocktails** vary from about 4% to above 12%. A 12-ounce can at 8% is 1.6 standard drinks, and at 12% it's 2.4.
- **Large-format cans** (19.2, 24, and 25-ounce "tallboys") of flavored malt beverages can contain four or more standard drinks in a single can.

The easiest habit: read the ABV and size before you open it, and do the quick math (ounces × ABV ÷ 0.6). Sweet and bubbly drinks are easy to drink fast, and that's when people underestimate. Our [hard seltzer hangover guide](/never-hungover/hard-seltzer-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) explains why these feel lighter than they are.

## Standard Drink by Country: Why the Number Isn't the Same Everywhere

There is no single international standard drink. Each country chose its own size, so "one drink" means different amounts depending on where the advice comes from.

| Country or region | One standard drink (pure alcohol) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| United States | 14 g | Used by NIAAA, CDC, and the Dietary Guidelines |
| Canada | about 13.5 g | 12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of 12% wine, 1.5 oz of 40% spirits |
| Australia | 10 g | Labels must state the number of standard drinks |
| New Zealand | 10 g | Labels also state standard drinks |
| United Kingdom | 8 g (one "unit") | 10 mL of pure alcohol; units are printed on many labels |
| World Health Organization | 10 g | Used in many WHO tools and screening questionnaires |

Some countries, such as Japan, have traditionally used a larger unit of about 20 grams. So "one drink" can range from 8 grams to 20 grams depending on which country's advice you're reading.

This matters when you compare guidelines across borders. The UK guideline of no more than **14 units a week** sounds similar to US numbers, but 14 UK units is 112 grams of alcohol, which works out to about **8 US standard drinks**. Australia's guideline of no more than **10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day** is 100 grams a week, or about 7 US drinks. When an article quotes "drinks per week" without saying whose drinks, the number can be off by almost double.

## What the Guidelines Say in Standard Drinks

These are summaries of official guidance. They describe levels of risk, not safe amounts, and every major body now says that drinking less is better for health than drinking more.

- **United States:** the 2020 to 2025 Dietary Guidelines for Americans advised that adults who choose to drink limit intake to **2 drinks or less a day for men and 1 drink or less a day for women**, on days when alcohol is consumed. They also said people who don't drink shouldn't start for health reasons. US guidance on alcohol has been under review, so check current federal advice for updates.
- **NIAAA definitions of heavy drinking:** for men, more than 4 drinks on any day or more than 14 a week; for women, more than 3 on any day or more than 7 a week.
- **Binge drinking (NIAAA):** a pattern that brings blood alcohol to 0.08% or higher, which for a typical adult means about **5 or more drinks for men or 4 or more for women in about two hours.**
- **United Kingdom:** the Chief Medical Officers advise not regularly drinking more than **14 units a week**, spread over three or more days, with several drink-free days.
- **Canada:** Canada's 2023 Guidance on Alcohol and Health describes **2 standard drinks or fewer a week** as low risk, 3 to 6 as moderate risk, and 7 or more as increasingly high risk.
- **Australia:** no more than **10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day.**

None of these limits apply to people who are pregnant or trying to become pregnant, people under the legal drinking age, people taking medications that interact with alcohol, or anyone planning to drive.

## Standard Drinks and Your Body: Timing, BAC, and How Long It Takes to Clear

Standard drinks are useful because your body processes alcohol at a fairly steady pace. A healthy adult's liver clears very roughly **one standard drink per hour**, which corresponds to blood alcohol falling by about 0.015% per hour. That rate varies with genetics, body size, liver health, and how much you drink regularly, and nothing you do the next morning (coffee, a cold shower, sweating it out) speeds it up in a meaningful way.

That gives you two practical rules:

1. **Pacing:** drinking more than one standard drink an hour means alcohol builds up in your blood faster than you clear it. Your blood alcohol keeps rising for a while after your last drink, so how you feel in the moment lags behind where you'll be in 30 to 90 minutes. Our guide on [how long it takes for alcohol to kick in](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-for-alcohol-to-kick-in) explains the lag.
2. **Clearing:** if you've had six standard drinks, assume it will take roughly six hours or more, counted from when you started, for your body to process them, and longer if your drinks were bigger than you thought. See [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) for the details, and [what BAC is](/never-hungover/what-is-bac) for how blood alcohol is measured.

Standard drinks also don't hit everyone the same way. A smaller person has less body water to dilute the same 14 grams, so their blood alcohol rises higher. Women, on average, reach higher blood alcohol than men after the same number of drinks. Drinking on an empty stomach makes alcohol reach the bloodstream faster. If you want a rough personal estimate, our [blood alcohol calculator](/never-hungover/blood-alcohol-calculator) uses standard drinks, body weight, and time. Treat any estimate as an approximation, never as permission to drive.

## Why Counting Standard Drinks Helps With Hangovers

Hangovers track the total amount of alcohol you drink much more closely than the type of drink. Two people who each had "four drinks" can wake up feeling very differently if one had four 12-ounce light beers (about 3.4 standard drinks) and the other had four 9-ounce pours of 14% wine (about 8.4 standard drinks). Counting in standard drinks explains a lot of "I only had a few" mornings.

Practical ways to use standard drinks on a night out:

- **Decide your number in advance** in standard drinks, not glasses, and convert as you go.
- **Choose lower-strength options** when you want to stay out longer: a 4% beer instead of an 8% one, or a spritz instead of a full glass of wine.
- **Use smaller glasses and measured pours** at home. A jigger costs a few dollars and removes most of the guesswork.
- **Alternate with water** and eat a real meal before and during drinking. Neither cancels out alcohol, but both slow how fast your blood alcohol rises and help you keep pace with one drink an hour.
- **Watch the "invisible" drinks:** refilled wine glasses, punch bowls, and large-format cans are the easiest to lose track of.

Counting also helps if you're keeping an eye on calories. Each standard drink carries about 98 calories from the alcohol alone (14 grams × 7 calories per gram), before any sugar from mixers or residual sugar in wine. Our [calories in alcohol guide](/never-hungover/calories-in-alcohol) breaks this down by drink.

For the habits that make the biggest difference to how you feel the next day, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## When to Worry: Signs a Night Has Gone Too Far

Most nights of moderate drinking end with nothing worse than a rough morning. But counting standard drinks also helps you notice when a night has gone well past normal, for you or for a friend.

**Call 911 (in the US) or your local emergency number right away** if someone who has been drinking:

- Can't be woken up, or is confused and can't respond normally
- Is vomiting while very drowsy or unconscious
- Has slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or long gaps between breaths
- Has a seizure
- Has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin, or a low body temperature

Don't leave them to "sleep it off." Lay them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, stay with them, and let emergency services know how much they drank if you can. Blood alcohol can keep rising after someone stops drinking, so a person who seems "just drunk" can get worse over the next hour.

Also talk to a doctor if you notice that you regularly need more drinks to feel the same effect, or that you feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or unwell when you haven't had a drink for a day or so. Those can be signs that your body has adapted to regular alcohol, and stopping suddenly after heavy daily drinking can be medically risky. A doctor can help you cut back safely, with no judgment.

## Where DHM Fits In (Honestly)

Counting standard drinks is the most reliable tool you have for a better next morning, because hangovers mostly come down to how much alcohol you drink and how fast. No supplement changes that.

Some people who drink socially also add **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's best viewed as promising rather than settled. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers your blood alcohol, makes it safe to drink more, or makes it safe to drive. If you'd like to try it alongside sensible pacing, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

A US standard drink is 14 grams of pure alcohol: about 12 ounces of 5% beer, 5 ounces of 12% wine, or 1.5 ounces of 40% liquor. Real drinks often contain more than that, because beers are stronger, wine pours are bigger, and cocktails contain multiple shots. To count any drink, multiply the ounces by the ABV and divide by 0.6. Use that number, not the number of glasses, when you think about pacing, limits, driving, and how you'll feel tomorrow. And remember that other countries use different sizes, so a UK unit or an Australian standard drink is smaller than an American one.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is considered one standard drink?**

In the US, one standard drink contains 14 grams (about 0.6 fluid ounces) of pure alcohol. That's roughly 12 ounces of regular beer at 5%, 5 ounces of wine at 12%, 8 to 9 ounces of malt liquor at 7%, or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof liquor. Stronger or larger drinks count as more than one.

**How do I calculate how many standard drinks are in a drink?**

Multiply the drink's size in ounces by its ABV as a decimal, then divide by 0.6. For example, a 16-ounce beer at 7% is 16 × 0.07 ÷ 0.6, or about 1.9 standard drinks. In milliliters, multiply mL × ABV × 0.789 to get grams of alcohol, then divide by 14 for US standard drinks.

**Is a pint of beer one standard drink?**

Usually not. A US pint is 16 ounces, so a pint of 5% beer is about 1.3 standard drinks, and a pint of 7% IPA is about 1.9. A British imperial pint is 568 mL, which at 5% is about 1.6 US standard drinks or 2.8 UK units.

**Is a glass of wine one standard drink?**

Only if it's a 5-ounce pour of about 12% wine. Many wines are 13.5 to 15%, and restaurant pours are often 6 ounces, while home pours can reach 8 or 9 ounces. A 9-ounce glass of 13.5% wine is about two standard drinks.

**How many standard drinks are in a bottle of wine?**

A 750 mL bottle at 12% contains about 5 US standard drinks. At 13.5% it's about 5.7, and at 15% it's more than 6. In the UK, a 13.5% bottle is about 10 units.

**What is the difference between a standard drink and a UK unit?**

A UK unit is 10 mL, or 8 grams, of pure alcohol. A US standard drink is 14 grams, so one US standard drink equals about 1.75 UK units. The UK's 14-units-a-week guideline works out to about 8 US standard drinks.

**How many standard drinks are in a shot?**

A 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof (40%) liquor is exactly one US standard drink. Higher-proof spirits, larger shot glasses, and bar pours of 1.25 to 2 ounces can change that. A double is at least two standard drinks.

**How long does it take to process one standard drink?**

A healthy adult clears very roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies with genetics, body size, liver health, and drinking habits. Coffee, cold showers, and exercise don't speed it up in any meaningful way. Only time lowers your blood alcohol.
